INTRODUCTION
         I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry, having been authorized
by the Committee, hereby present this One Hundred Thirty-second Report on the "MoU performance in respect of PSUs
of Power Sector, Department of Public Enterprises (Ministry of Heavy Industries and Public Enterprises)".
2.      The Sub-Committee for Ministry of Heavy Industries and Public Enterprises was constituted on the 6th January,
2003. This Sub-Committee has been examining the performance of MoU system in the PSUs and this report deals with
the performance of PSUs of the Power Sector.
3.      The report is based on the deliberations of the meetings held with the representatives of various PSUs and the oral
evidence of representatives of various Ministries at New Delhi on 5th August, 2003 and Chennai on 21st September,
2003.
4.      The Committee at its meeting held on 18th December, 2003 considered and adopted the Report..

REPORT
CHAPTER-I
MoU SYSTEM
1.      The Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) is a negotiated document between the Government, acting as the
owner of Public Sector Enterprise (PSE) and a specific PSE. It contains the intentions, obligations and mutual
responsibilities of the Government and the PSE. Further, MoU makes an attempt to move the management of PSEs from
management by controls and procedures to management by results and objectives.
1.2    The genesis of the policy of Memorandum of Understanding can be traced to the report of the Arjun Sengupta
Committee. One of the recommendations of this Committee was for the introduction of the system of MoU for
measurement of performance of public enterprises.
OBJECTIVES OF THE MoU SYSTEM
1.3    The objectives of the MoU system are to improve the performance of public enterprises by increasing autonomy
and accountability of the management; to remove the fuzziness in the goals and objectives of the enterprise to pursue
through clearly laid down performance targets in the MoU and to enable the evaluation of managerial performance
through objective criteria and provide a mechanism to reward good performance through performance incentives to
stimulate improved performance.

1.4    Under the agreement the enterprises undertake to achieve the targets set in the agreement at the beginning of the
year. Thus the MoU covers both financial performance as well as non-financial performance. Under this system
performance of the Company is categorized into five categories namely; excellent, very good, good, fair, and poor.
PREPARATION OF MoU
1.5    Based on the guidelines issued by the Department of Public Enterprises (DPE) in the month of October/November,
the draft MoUs are prepared by PSEs and forwarded to the Administrative Ministry and DPE by December. The draft
MoUs indicate the performance targets on a five point scale as proposed by the PSE for the ensuring financial year for
all crucial parameters like production, sales, profits, etc. The PSEs are also expected to include dynamic parameters of
significance for strengthening the future potential of the enterprise, such as project implementation, R&D, Human
Resource Development, etc. Appropriate weights are assigned to each of these parameters. The draft MoU are discussed
with the PSE Administrative Ministries at the Adhoc Task Force (ATF) negotiation meetings arranged in DPE in the
month of March/April, soon after the presentation of the Union Budget. Since the Budget has implications on the
performance targets, the timing of the negotiation meetings is deliberately scheduled after the budget presentation. The
appropriateness of the parameters and weights and the soundness of the targets as also the commitments of the
Government are examined in detail at the negotiation meetings. The draft MoUs as finalised thereafter are placed before
the High Power Committee (HPC) comprising the Cabinet Secretary as Chairman, Secretary, Finance. Planning
Commission, Programme Implementation, Chairman Public Enterprises Selection Board, Chief Economic Adviser and
Secretary Public Enterprises as Members, for approval. After approval, they are signed by the respective Chief
Executives and Secretaries.
EVALUATION OF MoU
1.6    The evaluation of the MoU signing enterprises is done at the end of the year by the Ad-hoc Task Force (ATF) on
the basis of actual achievement vis-a-vis the MoU targets. Where the performance exceeds the targets by the pre-
determined stipulated level the enterprise is ranked as ‘excellent’ and when the target is just met, the enterprise is ranked
as ‘very good’. In other cases, where the targets are not met the enterprise is ranked either ‘good’ or ‘fair’ or ‘poor’.
Ranking depends on how the performance has been as compared to MoU targets.
1.7    The performance criteria should be assigned appropriate weights corresponding with their stated priorities in the
objectives. It should be ensured that they also reflect the perceived relative importance of the various criteria in the
judgement of the PSE/Ministry. The weight for physical criteria should be kept as low as possible. Instead, Efficiency
and Dynamic criteria should get higher weights. The weight for profit-related financial parameters would be 60% in
case of PSEs operating under free market mechanism. The weight of 60% would be distributed to, Gross Margin, Gross
Profit/Capital Employed and Net Profit/Net Worth, each having a weight of 20% each. For PSEs operating under
administered prices, PSEs where Government is sole/almost sole customer and Trading, Consultancy, Engineering and
Financial PSEs, the weight would be 40%. The weight of 40% would be distributed to, Gross Margin and Net Profit/Net
Worth, each having a weight of 20% each. The PSEs which have been specially set up for implementing certain
Government policy directives will have no pre-determined financial parameters.
1.8    The targets set should be realistic and growth oriented. It should be insured that the MoU targets flow from the
Corporate Vision/Plans formulated by the PSEs and there is linkage between them. In case there is any variation,
reasons thereof should be clearly specified. For qualitative indicators, the targets for each of the points on the 5-point
scale should be indicated in the performance matrix itself. If these targets are on a time scale, only such target which fall
within the MoU year is included.
1.9    The MOU should contain the past five years performance data on criteria included in the MoU in an appendix. It
should also indicate the projections for the next five years, as far as possible consistent with the corporate plan.
POWER SECTOR
1.10  Power is a critical infrastructure for economic development and for improving the quality of life. The achievement
of increasing installed power capacity from 1362 MW to over 100,000 MW since independence and electrification of
more than 500,00 villages is impressive in absolute terms. However, it is a matter of concern that the annual per capita
consumption of India, at about 350 kwh is among the lowest in the world. Further, people in a large number of villages
have no access to electricity. The end users of electricity like households, farmers, commercial establishments,
industries are confronted with frequent power cuts, both scheduled and unscheduled. Power cuts, erratic voltage and low
or high supply frequency have added to the power woes of the consumer. These problems emanate from:---
         (i)     Inadequate power generation capacity;
         (ii)     Lack of optimum utilization of the existing generation capacity;

CHAPTER-II
NATIONAL THERMAL POWER CORPORATION LIMITED (NTPC)
2.0    The National Thermal Power Corporation Limited (NTPC) was incorporated in November, 1975 with the
objective of planning, promoting and organizing integrated development of thermal power in the country and has a
Vision: “To be one of the World’s largest and best power utilities, powering India’s growth”. NTPC is schedule ‘A’
Navratan Company having a total approved investment of Rs.63,242.16 crores. NTPC has an approved capacity of
26,755 MW. The authorized capital of the Corporation is Rs.10,000 crores.
2.1    The Corporation has under operation/implementation coal based super thermal power plants/projects at thirteen
locations namely Singrauli (UP), Rihand (UP), NCTPP Dadri (UP), Korba (Chhattisgarh), Vindhyachal (MP),
Ramagundam (AP), Farakka (WB), Kahalgaon (Bihar), Talcher-Kaniha (Orissa), Talcher (Orissa), Unchahar (UP).
Simhadri (A.P.) and Tanda (UP) and combined cycle gas power projects at seven locations namely Anta (Rajasthan),
Auraiya (UP), Dadri (UP), Kawas (Gujarat), Jhanor-Gandhar (Gujarat), Kayamkulam (Kerala) and Faridabad
(Haryana). In addition NTPC is implementing its first hydro electric power project namely Koldam HEPP (800 MW).
The NTPC has already commissioned 20,935 MW. In addition to this, NTPC has taken over 314 MW of Captive power
Plants at Durgapur, Rourkela and Bhilai Steel Plants of SAIL through formation of 50:50 equity participation Joint
ventures between NTPC and SAIL. Thus, the total installed capacity of NTPC is 21249 MW. Apart from this, Badarpur
Thermal Power Station (705 MW), which is a major source of power supply to Delhi is being managed by NTPC on
behalf of Government of India.

over a period of time, with reference to the MoU system that was introduced, improvements were made in this
instrument itself. And today, the NTPC is not only a Navratna but has become a Navratna Company sanctioning its own
projects. Since this instrument was introduced, the NTPC has always been categorised in the group of excellent
performers. They have emerged as one of the top most power-generating companies in the world.

2.30  The Committee was informed that the MoU instrument, which was started with some parameters in the beginning,
over a period of time, it captured various parameters like R&D, ash utilisation, environment, technological improvement
and upgradation, efficiency, technical resources, commercial resources and financial resources, not only gross margin
but also profit as a ratio to the net worth. These performance parameters of the NTPC are brought into focus and they
have been continuously improved upon. Whatever commitments were made NTPC tried to meet the commitments.
Sometimes, it required coordination, sanction and approval of other Ministries and Departments which were
continuously tried to get. After attaining the Navaratna status, the Board of NTPC was also professionalised and reduced
the number of Government Directors on the Board from what it used to be in the past, and brought people from outside,
from the financial side, from the technology side and from the professional management side.
2.31  The Committee observes that the MoU rating in respect of NTPC over the last 16 years have been graded as
excellent this kind of rating needs to be modified in view of the power scenario in the country. i.e. Gross generation of
Power and requirement. It is a fact that NTPC is the bulk power generator in the Country. However, power supply of
country still fall short of the requirement. In view of this, excellent rating seems to be a misnomer. The Committee

POWER GRID CORPORATION OF INDIA LIMITED (PGCIL)
4.0    PGCIL is the largest and best managed transmission utilities in the world. It was incorporated in October, 1989 for
establishment and operation of regional and national power grids, through transfer of transmission assets and manpower
from the constituent central sector undertakings namely NTPC, NEPC, NFEPCO etc. PGCIL started commercial
operation in 1992-93 and now the Company owns and operates about 46,245 ckt kms of transmission lines at 765 kV,
400 kV, 220 kV & 132 kV levels and 79 sub-stations with transformation capacity of about 44,736 MVA. The
transmission system availability is maintained consistently over 98.5% by deploying best Operation and Maintenance
practices at par with the global standards. About 40% of total power generated in the country, more than 200 billion
units worth Rs.40,000 crore per year, is being transmitted across the country over PGCIL’s transmission network.
PGCIL has been accorded ‘Mini Navratna’ status w.e.f. 14th October, 1998.
4.1    PGCIL has an impressive track record of financial performance as well. The turnover went up from a modest
Rs.634 crore in 1992-93 to Rs.2,533 crore in 2002-03, registering an average annual growth rate of 26%. It registered a
net profit of Rs.643 crore in 2002-03 as against Rs.236 crore in 1992-93 thereby establishing an annual growth rate of
about 16%.
4.2    PGCIL has in-house expertise in all specialised areas of power transmission with systems upto 800 KV EHV AC,
± 500 KV HVDC, Gas Insulated Sub-stations, Static Var Compensation, Series Capacitors, Controlled Shunt Reactors
etc. Towards dovetailing R&D activities into practice, it has tied up with various renowned Academic/Research
institutes like IITs (Indian Institute of Technology), CPRI (Central Power Research Institute), etc. Based upon its
expertise in the areas of Engineering, Contracting, Project Management, Financial management, etc., it has bagged
many national and international consultancy projects.
4.3    PGCIL has adopted one of the highly effective disaster management mechanism through deployment of
Emergency Restoration System (FRS) to minimise the adverse impact on transmission system caused by natural
calamities like flood, cyclone, earthquake etc. The devastation caused by cyclone in Gujarat in June, 1998, Orissa in
October, 1999 and earthquake in Gujarat in January, 2001 were attended by PGCIL on war footing and normalcy was
restored within few days, which otherwise would have taken several months. PGCIL has been recognized as the nodal
agency for disaster management in Indian power sector. It is the first power utility in India to evolve Environmental and
Social Policy & Procedures (ESPP) through public interactions and is implementing the ESPP in its transmission
projects in letter and spirit.
4.4    PGCIL has planned to create a strong and vibrant National Power Grid in a phased manner to ensure optimum
utilization generating resources, conservation of eco sensitive right of way and for having flexibility to accommodate
the uncertainty of generation plans. Commissioning of 500 MW Sasaram HVDC back to back link interconnecting
Eastern Region with Northern Region marked the completion of first phase of the National Grid with 5000 MW inter-
regional power transfer capacity. Under the first phase, all the power regions of the country have been interlinked
mainly through asynchronous HVDC links.
4.5    The commissioning of second phase of the National Grid has already begun with the commissioning of 2000 MW
Talcher-Kolar bi-polar HVDC link, achieved 9 months ahead of schedule and at a cost lower by Rs.700 crore than the
approved cost. Early commissioning of this project enabled transfer of surplus power from Eastern Region to Southern
Region. The 400 KV D/C Raipur-Rourkela line (East- West Interconnector) was commissioned in March 2003, thereby
enhancing the cumulative inter-regional power transfer capacity to 8000 MW. This project has been commissioned one
year ahead of schedule. Early commissioning of this line has facilitated transfer of surplus power of Eastern Region.
This also marks the synchronous operation of regional grids covering North-Eastern, Eastern, and Western Regions with
a combined installed capacity of 50,000 MW stretching from Arunachal Pradesh in North Eastern Region to Goa in
Western Region, i.e. a distance of more than 2500 KM. The second phase of National Grid consisting of a hybrid
system of HVDC & 765 kV systems shall be completed by the year 2007, when the inter-regional power transfer
capacity is envisaged to be about 23,500 MW depending upon completion of planned generation projects.

4.22  The Committee observes that the lengthy procedure in the process of approval of projects and the delays involved
should be minimized which is a severe constraint in the functioning of any PSUs in terms of MoU. The Committee
stressed that the Government should simplify the procedure involved to avoid the delay in approval of national level
projects.

and nearly 20% of the spares are imported which involves imposition of customs duty and it adversely affects the list of
projects. The representatives of PGCIL apprised the Committee that the import duty has been adversely affecting
PGCIL and exemption should be given to them as ‘The case of BHEL which is given in terms of mega projects.
4.24  The Committee, therefore recommends that the case of PGCIL should be sympathetically considered by the
Government for import duty exemption on the lines of BHEL which is given in terms of Mega project.
4.25  The Committee also observes that the further growth potential in the core area of EHV transmission should
be fully utilized by the Government and thereby the target of National Grid would be achieved by the year 2012.
4.26  The Committee further observes that the potentials in the area of long distance communication and use of
optic fibre and state of the art technology should be fully exploited.
4.27  The Committee was apprised about the transmission loss which is 4.5% at par with the world standard. However,
the distribution loss is pinching the power sector as a whole, which is at 40% against the 5 to 8% of the world standard.

grid failures.
4.28  The Committee observes that such losses can be reduced by better management and adopting the state of
art the technology available in the global arena. The Committee further observes that the role of State Electricity
Boards can not be ruled out in achieving the speedy implementation of the ongoing distribution reform
programmes.

OBSERVATIONS/RECOMMENDATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE AT A GLANCE
         The Committee observes that the MoU rating in respect of NTPC over the last 16 years have been graded as
excellent this kind of rating needs to be modified in view of the power scenario in the country. i.e. Gross generation of
Power and requirement. It is a fact that NTPC is the bulk power generator in the Country. However, power supply of
country still fall short of the requirement. In view of this, excellent rating seems to be a misnomer. The Committee,
therefore, recommends that MoU ratio in respect of NTPC should be integrated with the actual need of the power of the
Country and production. Targets should be fixed in the national perspective.                                                             (Para
: 2.31)
         The Committee observes that although NTPC have taken measures to attain optimum growth of the Company by
taking several measures like reducing the number of Government Directors on the Board, and inducting professional
from finance and technology side to improve its efficiency but there is still scope for improvement although the
Company has a happy experience of working along the MoU instrument. In view of the increasing global
competitiveness MoU parameters for NTPC should be modified to raise it to the status of the global Company that
NTPC needs to attain in the present scenario of liberlisation of
economy.                                                                                   (Para : 2.32)
         The Committee observed that the growth criteria for power generation under MoU should be measured year after
year and not from what it was since its inception i.e. 1998-99 if the growth percentage is based from year to year, the
growth trend of this Company is not very encouraging. It is reflected in the gross generation and the total requirement of
the power in the Country. MoU system should be framed in such a way so as to exhibit growth trend year after year and
encourage and invite it. Projects should be completed with in a fixed time frame.                                        (Para : 2.34)
         The Committee observes that notwithstanding the excellent performance and improvement in the generation of
power, human productivity index should be evaluated in terms of international scale. In the Indian context, human
productivity index may be excellent but this should be comparably to average human productivity at the global scene.
MoU parameters should see to it that human productivity can be raised to optimum level and may be brought at par with
the international standards.         (Para : 2.36)
         As regards the environmental criteria where NTPC has qualitative parameters in which the main parameter relates
to ash utilisation. NTPC has been trying to improve ash utilisation in their plants progressively. The Committee is happy
to note that the Centre for Power Efficiency Environment Protection (CENPEEP) promoted by the NTPC is playing a
major role in the Development of eco-friendly and eco-nurturing initiative towards environmental protection and
continued to sustainable power development in India. The committee feels that CENPEEP should be fully exploited so
as to ensure clean environment.                                                                                                                      (Para : 2.37)

incorporated in the weightages assigned to MoU parameters the Committee observes that the weightage assigned to the
Financial Parameters under MoU may be revised to 60% from present level of 40%.                          (Para : 3.6)

generation and the skill should be properly utilized and further the Company should avail the opportunities in this regard

sufficiency in the power sector and should not get complacent.                                                                (Para : 3.11)

Generation should be utilized effectively. The Committee is however of the view that the feasibilities for Lignite
Projects in other parts of the Country should be explored.                                                                   (Para : 3.13)
